note_tweet.text:
Nvidia reportedly asked TSMC to explore making 3D DRAM. 

"FAKE NEWS" was my knee-jerk reaction, but perhaps that's too strong.

Whatever's going on, it is NOT a near-term fix for the DRAM shortage.

TSMC is a logic chip maker, not a DRAM manufacturer - VERY different production requirements.

Patents show TSMC has explored 3D DRAM designs, but R&D and patents are a long way from mass production. 

TSMC can't simply convert a logic fab and start shipping. Equipment overlap helps, but developing the production process, qualifying the product and bringing it to mass production would be a multiyear undertaking.

Where does the specialized memory production technology come from? A licensing deal with a major memory maker? An acquisition? A JV? Otherwise, developing its own competitive 3D DRAM production process could take several years.

And even a licensing deal would not make production instant. Integration, qualification and yield still have to be solved.

note_tweet.text:
Much of the economic data we use to understand the world, such as the incomes people receive, is recorded in the local currencies of each country. On their own, numbers in local currencies tell us nothing about how they compare. One obvious approach would be to convert them into a common currency using market exchange rates. But this doesn’t give us the comparison we often look for: what money can actually buy in different countries. This is because the cost of living varies a lot across countries.

International dollars are a hypothetical currency that aims to have the same purchasing power everywhere. They are adjusted for differences in living costs across countries and price changes over time. Wherever it is “spent”, one international dollar buys the same goods and services as one US dollar would in the United States.

Making incomes comparable across countries matters especially for our understanding of global inequality. Using market dollars — local currencies converted to US dollars using market exchange rates — to compare incomes across countries understates people’s real income in countries where local prices are often much lower than in the US.

Take India, for example. Its gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is almost 30 times lower than that of the US in market dollars. But when we adjust for differences in living costs, the gap shrinks to about eight times lower. For Burkina Faso, the difference is even starker: its GDP per capita is 83 times lower than that of the US in market dollars, and 30 times lower after adjusting for differences in living costs. Global inequality remains large, even after accounting for what people can buy locally.

Tuesday's election results will have sweeping impacts on America's data center boom. 

Our team at Cleanview analyzed the data and found that newly elected governors could pause 41% of America’s planned data centers. 

Here are some more takeaways from last night's results:

On Tuesday, voters elected governors and passed local measures that will change the course of the AI infrastructure boom. But much of the early coverage has been misleading or wrong. 

Tuesday’s results don’t signal the end of the data center boom. They will, however, likely bring a pause in some of the largest markets and new regulations across the country—even in traditionally laissez-faire states like Texas.

159 GW of planned data centers are in states where the new governor backs a pause. That's 41% of the country's planned data center pipeline. 

Another 69.2 GW (18%) is in states where the winner wants to change tax breaks or other rules but hasn’t backed a pause.

This week’s elections will also impact the power projects that data centers depend on, likely bringing more clean energy in some states and fewer on-site gas plants in others.

On-site gas plants will likely face new rules and delays. To build an on-site gas plant, a developer needs an air permit. That approval often goes through offices controlled by the executive branch, which means new Democratic governors could delay or block those permits.

Developers may need to buy more clean energy. A number of candidates campaigned on a promise to make data centers buy more clean energy.

David Crowley in Wisconsin called for 100% renewable energy as a condition for communities that accept a project. Haaland’s plan calls for self-built renewables. Michigan Democrats have proposed a bill requiring 90% clean procurement.

Another takeaway from last night: Local elections went overwhelmingly against data centers. 

Data centers were directly on the ballot in 41 local elections across the country. Some ballot initiatives proposed outright bans, while others proposed temporary pauses. All of the races that have been called went against data centers. 

Many questions remain about how many newly elected officials will follow through with their pauses, how long they'll last, which projects will be affected, and what new guardrails would look like. 

We're planning to continue to cover this over the coming months. If you're interested in reading our analysis subscribe to the Cleanview newsletter or follow along here.
